TENTATIVE RULINGS FOR March 5th. 2026
Department R17- Judge Gilbert G. Ochoa
This court follows California Rules of Court, rule 3.1308(a) (1) for tentative rulings. (See San Bernardino
Superior Court Local Emergency Rule 8.) Tentative rulings for each law & motion will be posted on the
internet (https://www.sb-court.org) by 3:00 p.m. on the court day immediately before the hearing.
If you do not have internet access or if you experience difficulty with the posted tentative ruling, you may
obtain the tentative ruling by calling the Administrative Assistant. You may appear in person at the
hearing but personal appearance is not required and remote appearance by CourtCall is preferred during
the Pandemic. (See www.sbcourt.org/general-information/remote-access)
If you wish to submit on the ruling, call the Court, check-in and state that you will be submitting on
the Tentative, and your appearance is not necessary. But you must check in.
If both sides do not appear, the tentative will simply become the ruling.
If any party submits on the tentative, the Court will not alter the tentative and it will become the
ruling.
If one party wants to argue, Court will hear argument but will not change the tentative.
If the Court does decide to modify tentative after argument, then a further hearing for oral
argument will be reset for both parties to be heard at the same time by the Court.
This procedure is meant to minimize your waiting time in Court and to get you on your way.
PRESTON
V.
CENTRAL SCHOOL DISTRICT, ET AL.
CIVRS2402011
Motion: Demurrer to Second Amended Complaint
Movant: Defendant Central School District
Respondent: Plaintiff Rahshana Preston
I. DISCUSSION
a. Meet and Confer Requirement
Under Code of Civil Procedure section 430.41, subdivision (a), before filing a demurrer,
the objecting party shall meet and confer with the opposing party for the purpose of determining
whether an agreement can be reached to resolve the objections to the pleading. The parties
should meet and confer at least five days before the responsive pleading is due. Under Code of
Page | 1
Civil Procedure section 430.41, subdivision (a)(3), the demurring party must file a declaration
stating either:
(A) The means by which the demurring party met and conferred with the party who
filed the pleading subject to demurrer, and that the parties did not reach an
agreement resolving the objections raised in the demurrer.
(B) That the party who filed the pleading subject to demurrer failed to respond to
the meet and confer request of the demurring party or otherwise failed to meet and
confer in good faith.
Defense counsel, Matthew Soleimanpour, declares that he sent Plaintiff’s counsel a meet
and confer letter, but that Plaintiff’s counsel refused to engage in the meet and confer process.
(See Soleimanpour Decl. ¶¶3-7.) Plaintiff’s counsel’s position is that she sufficiently met and
conferred in the process of the parties’ stipulation to file the SAC. (See Patel Decl. ¶¶5-14.)
The declarations of counsel establish that the parties failed to meet and confer “in person,
by telephone, or by video conference,” as required by statute. (See Code Civ. Proc., § 430.41,
subd. (a).) The motion is off calendar and both parties are ordered to comply with the Code.
Movant to give Notice.
Dated-

Judge

v.
SALVADOR HERANDEZ dba HERNANDEZ NURSERY, et al.
CIVRS2503212
Motion(s): (1) Demurrer to FACC
Movant(s): Plaintiff / Cross-Defendant Dalia Lopez
Respondent(s): Defendant / Cross-Complainant Chino Valley Growers
______________________________________________________
Motion(s): (2) Demurrer to FACC
Movant(s): Plaintiff / Cross-Defendant Dalia Lopez
Respondent(s): Defendant / Cross-Complainant Salvador Hernandez dba Hernandez
Nursery
______________________________________________________________________
Page | 3
Demurrer to CVG’s FACC - First Cause of Action: Conversion
Conversion is any act of dominion wrongfully exerted over another’s personal property, in
denial of, or inconsistent with, the other person’s rights. (Messerall v. Fulwider (1988) 199
Cal.App.3d 1324, 1329; Oakes v. Suelynn Corp. (1972) 24 Cal.App.3d 271, 278.) In order to
establish conversion, plaintiff must show an intention or purpose to convert the goods and to
exercise ownership or dominion over them, or to prevent the owner from taking possession of his
or her property. (Collin v. American Empire Ins. Co. (1994) 21 Cal.App.th 787, 812.) Money
cannot be the subject of a cause of action for conversion unless there is a specific, identifiable sum
involved. (PCO, Inc. v. Christensen, Miller, Fink, Jacobs, Glaser, Weil & Shapiro, LLP (2007)
150 Cal.App.4th 384, 395.)
To plead conversion, a plaintiff must set forth the following allegations: (1) plaintiff’s right
to possession of personal property; (2) defendant’s significant interference with plaintiff’s right to
possession; (3) intentional or knowing interference; (4) plaintiff’s lack of consent; and (5)
consequent injury, damage, loss, or harm. (CACI No. 2100.)
Cross-Complainant CVG alleges that Hernandez owns CVG. Cross-Defendant Lopez was
never an employee or owner of CVG but held herself out as owner of CVG and sold CVG
inventory to third parties without knowledge or consent of Hernandez. CVG further alleges that
Lopez retained all sales proceeds and did not report the sales to CVG or Hernandez. As a result,
CVG was harmed. (FACC ¶¶ 14-19.)
Lopez argues that the FACC lacks specificity; CVG does not plead when the alleged
conversion happened, what the inventory is, the amount of inventory, the amount of damages, how
CVG learned of the alleged sales, or who the alleged sales were made to.
Page | 4
Here, CVG alleges that Hernandez owns CVG. The allegations address ownership of the
entity, not CVG’s right to possess the property allegedly converted. On the facts alleged, CVG
does not allege that it owned the inventory, had the immediate right to possess it, or otherwise had
a possessory interest in the property at the time Lopez allegedly sold it and retained proceeds.
Further, CVG’s conversion claim is insufficient to the extent that it seeks recovery of money
because it does not allege a specific, identifiable sum or otherwise allege that the funds are capable
of being traced. Instead, CVG alleges that Lopez sold inventory and “retained proceeds,” which
amounts to a generalized claim for damages rather than conversion of a particular, identifiable
fund.
Therefore, the Court sustains the demurrer, with 10 days leave to amend.
Demurrer to Hernandez’s FACC - First Cause of Action: Civil Extortion
“Extortion is the obtaining of property or other consideration from another, with his or
her consent ... induced by a wrongful use of force or fear.” (Pen. Code, § 518.) “Fear, such as will
constitute extortion, may be induced by a threat of any of the following: [¶] 1. To do an unlawful
injury to the person or property of the individual threatened or of a third person[;] [¶] 2. To accuse
the individual threatened ... of a crime[;] [¶] 3. To expose, or to impute to him ... a deformity,
disgrace, or crime[;] [¶] 4. To expose a secret affecting him, her, or them….” (Pen. Code, § 519.)”
(Tran v. Nguyen (2023) 97 Cal.App.5th 523, 529, reh’g denied (Dec. 19, 2023), review denied
(Mar. 12, 2024).) “The concept of coerced consent is at the heart of extortion.” (Ibid.; People v.
Goodman (1958) 159 Cal.App.2d 54, 61 [“To constitute extortion the victim must consent, albeit
it is a coerced and unwilling consent, to surrender of his property”].)
Civil extortion has been held to be a “cause of action for the recovery of money obtained
by the wrongful threat of criminal or civil prosecution. [Citations.] It is essentially a cause of
Page | 5
action for moneys obtained by duress, a form of fraud.” (Fuhrman v. California Satellite Systems,
Inc. (1986) 179 Cal.App.3d 408, 426 (Fuhrman), abrogated on other grounds in Silberg v.
Anderson (1990) 50 Cal.3d 205 (Silberg); see also, Stenehjem v. Sareen (2014) 226 Cal.App.4th
1405.) Under Penal Code section 518, subdivision (b), “consideration” means anything of value.
Cross-Complainant Hernandez alleges that he owned CVG. For two decades, Hernandez
and Lopez dated each other romantically. Lopez was never an employee of CVG. Hernandez
alleges that he consistently rejected Cross-Defendant Lopez’s demands that she should become his
business partner at CVG. Lopez threatened to reveal to Hernandez’s wife the long-term affair of
nearly two decades if Hernandez continued to deny Lopez with any interest in CVG. (FACC ¶¶
6-10.)
Lopez argues that the FACC is devoid of facts alleging that Lopez received any portion of
the business because Hernandez consistently rejected Lopez’s demands that she be his business
partner at CVG. Lopez argues that Hernandez’s civil extortion claim is thus fatally flawed because
she never “obtained” an interest in the business. Further, Lopez argues that Hernandez does not
allege that he felt fear of Lopez’s threat to expose their affair.
In opposition, Hernandez argues Lopez’s threat to reveal the affair was made to induce
Hernandez to give her an interest in CVG and argues that this constitutes “consideration” under
Penal Code section 518.
On the facts alleged, the claim asserted is not for extortion, but attempted extortion. Penal
Code section 524 proscribes attempted extortion, the elements of which are (1) a specific intent to
commit extortion, that is to obtain property from another, with his or her consent, induced by a
wrongful use of fear; and (2) a direct but ineffectual act done towards its commission. Here,
Hernandez does not allege that he ever parted with an ownership interest, paid money, transferred
Page | 6
inventory, or gave any other identifiable property right because of Lopez’s threat. To the contrary,
Hernandez alleges that he “consistently rejected” Lopez’s demands. (FACC ¶ 9.) There was no
action induced by Lopez’s threat and no transfer of property as a result. Without factual allegations
that Lopez obtained something of value, the extortion element is missing and the claim fails.
Further, an intent to induce Hernandez to act or the fact that a threat was made to pressure
him is the alleged means of conduct, not the consideration obtained. The intent to induce supports
an inference of an attempt to extort where the demand is rejected and nothing is transferred. No
authority is cited for the proposition that attempted extortion is a recognized civil cause of action.
To the contrary, in Fuhrman, supra, 179 Cal.App.3d at p. 426, disapproved on other grounds in
Silberg, supra, 50 Cal.3d 205, the Court of Appeal noted that the “fatal flaw” in the plaintiff’s
cause of action “is that she apparently never paid the money defendants demanded in their
[extortion] letters” and that had the plaintiff actually paid the money demanded, she would have
alleged legally sufficient damages because an extortion claim is essentially an action for “duress
to recover moneys received by a defendant under the influence of duress.” (Id. at p. 428.)
Therefore, the Court sustains the demurrer, without leave to amend, because the FACC
makes clear that the attempted extortion was consistently rejected. It is not demonstrated
Hernandez can amend to state a civil extortion cause of action against Lopez.
Rulings
(1) Demurrer to CVG’s FACC - First Cause of Action: Conversion
SUSTAIN Cross-Defendant Lopez’s demurrer to CVG’s first cause of action for
conversion, with 10 days leave to amend. CVG fails to allege sufficient facts in support of a
conversion cause of action.
Page | 7
(2) Demurrer to Hernandez’s FACC - First Cause of Action: Civil Extortion
SUSTAIN Cross-Defendant Lopez’s demurrer to Hernandez’s first cause of action for civil
extortion, without leave to amend. Cross-Complainant Hernandez does not allege actual transfer
of interest of CVG to Lopez; the cause of action for civil extortion is fatally flawed and amendment
would be futile.
Movant to give Notice.
Dated-
____________________________
Judge
